units.meaning: Section title designating 29 CFR 825.110 as governing eligible employees under the FMLA, containing no operative legal rules on its own.
An eligible employee under the FMLA must be an employee of a covered employer who has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months.

To be an eligible employee of a covered employer under the FMLA, the employee must have been employed for at least 1,250 hours of service during the 12-month period immediately preceding the commencement of the leave, subject to special hours of service requirements for airline flight crew employees under § 825.801.

To be an eligible employee of a covered employer under the FMLA, the employee must be employed at a worksite where 50 or more employees are employed by the employer within 75 miles of that worksite (referencing § 825.105(b) for employees working outside the U.S.).
The 12 months an employee must have been employed by the employer to be eligible for FMLA leave need not be consecutive months, provided the qualifying conditions of paragraph (b) are met.

In determining whether an employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months, employment periods prior to a break in service of seven years or more need not be counted, subject to the exceptions set forth in paragraph (b)(2).

Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted in determining whether the employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months where the employee's break in service is occasioned by the fulfillment of a USERRA-covered service obligation (38 U.S.C. 4301 et seq.); furthermore, the period of absence from work due to or necessitated by USERRA-covered service must also be counted, without providing any greater entitlement than would be available under USERRA.

Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted in determining whether the employee has been employed by the employer for at least 12 months where a written agreement, including a collective bargaining agreement, exists concerning the employer's intention to rehire the employee after the break in service (such as for the employee furthering education or for childrearing purposes).

If an employee is maintained on the payroll for any part of a week, including any periods of paid or unpaid leave (such as sick or vacation leave) during which other benefits or compensation are provided by the employer (such as workers' compensation or group health plan benefits), that week counts as a full week of employment.
For the purpose of determining whether intermittent, occasional, or casual employment qualifies as at least 12 months of employment, 52 weeks is deemed to be equal to 12 months.

Employers are not prevented from considering employment prior to a continuous break in service of more than seven years when determining whether an employee has met the 12-month employment requirement.

If an employer chooses to recognize employment prior to a continuous break in service of more than seven years, the employer must do so uniformly with respect to all employees with similar breaks in service.

Except as provided in paragraph (c)(2) and § 825.801 for airline flight crew employees, whether an employee has worked the minimum 1,250 hours of service is determined according to FLSA principles for determining compensable hours of work (29 CFR part 785), with the determining factor being the number of hours worked within the meaning of the FLSA, not limited by recordkeeping methods or inaccurate compensation agreements; any accurate accounting of actual hours worked under FLSA principles may be used.

An employee returning from USERRA-covered service must be credited with the hours of service that would have been performed but for the absence necessitated by USERRA-covered service when determining FMLA eligibility, adding those hours to any hours actually worked during the previous 12-month period to meet the hours of service requirement (with the pre-service work schedule generally usable for calculations, subject to § 825.801(c) for airline flight crew employees).

If an employer does not maintain an accurate record of hours worked by an employee, including employees exempt from FLSA recordkeeping requirements (such as bona fide executive, administrative, and professional employees under 29 CFR part 541), the employer bears the burden of showing that the employee has not worked the requisite 1,250 hours (for example, by clearly demonstrating that full-time teachers did not work 1,250 hours during the previous 12 months), subject to § 825.801(d) for airline flight crew employees.
The determination of whether an employee meets the hours of service requirement and has been employed for a total of at least 12 months must be made as of the date the FMLA leave is to start.

An employee may be on non-FMLA leave at the time the 12-month eligibility requirement is met, and in that event, any portion of the leave taken for an FMLA-qualifying reason after meeting the requirement is FMLA leave.
Whether 50 employees are employed within 75 miles to determine an employee's FMLA eligibility must be determined at the time the employee gives notice of the need for leave.

Once an employee is determined eligible in response to notice of the need for leave (whether taken at one time or on an intermittent or reduced leave schedule basis), the employee's eligibility for that specific notice is not affected by any subsequent drop or change in the number of employees within 75 miles of the worksite, and the employer may not terminate employee leave that has already started if the employee count drops below 50.

If an employer employs 50 or more employees (such as 60 employees in August) at the time an otherwise eligible employee gives notice of the need for leave, the employer must grant FMLA benefits for leave scheduled to begin later (such as December), even if the employer expects the employee count to drop below 50 (such as to 40 in December) before the leave begins.
Title heading for 29 CFR 825.110 designating the regulation governing eligible employees, possessing no substantive legal requirement on its own.

To be an eligible employee under the FMLA, an employee of a covered employer must meet three cumulative criteria: have been employed by that employer for at least 12 months; have been employed for at least 1,250 hours of service during the 12-month period immediately preceding the start of the leave (subject to special rules in § 825.801 for airline flight crew employees); and be employed at a worksite where 50 or more employees are employed by the employer within 75 miles of that worksite (referencing § 825.105(b) for employees outside the U.S.).
The 12 months of employment required for FMLA eligibility do not have to be consecutive, provided the governing conditions and rules regarding breaks in service under paragraph (b) are met.

When determining whether an employee has been employed for at least 12 months, employers are not required to count employment periods occurring prior to a break in service of seven years or more, unless one of the exceptions in paragraph (b)(2) applies.

Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted toward the 12-month employment requirement if the break was occasioned by fulfilling a USERRA-covered service obligation; furthermore, the period of absence necessitated by USERRA service must also be counted, provided this does not confer greater entitlement than available under USERRA.

Employment periods preceding a break in service of more than seven years must be counted toward the 12-month employment requirement if a written agreement (such as a collective bargaining agreement) exists expressing the employer's intention to rehire the employee after the break in service (for instance, to further education or for childrearing).

A week is deemed to count as a week of employment toward the 12-month requirement if an employee is on the payroll for any part of that week, including periods of paid or unpaid leave (such as sick leave or vacation) in which the employer provides other benefits or compensation (such as workers' compensation or group health plan benefits).
For intermittent, occasional, or casual employment, 52 weeks of qualifying employment is legally deemed to satisfy the 12 months of employment requirement.

Employers are permitted, at their discretion, to count employment that occurred prior to a continuous break in service exceeding seven years even when not required by paragraphs (b)(2)(i) or (b)(2)(ii).

If an employer exercises the option to credit employment prior to a break in service of more than seven years beyond statutory requirements, it must do so uniformly across all employees having similar breaks in service.

Except as provided in paragraph (c)(2) and § 825.801 for airline flight crew employees, whether an employee satisfies the 1,250 hours of service threshold must be determined under FLSA principles for compensable hours worked (29 CFR part 785), with the determinative factor being the actual number of hours worked for the employer within the meaning of the FLSA.

The calculation of compensable hours is not constrained by specific recordkeeping methods or inaccurate compensation agreements; any accurate accounting of actual hours worked under FLSA principles is permissible to establish hours of service.

An employee returning from USERRA-covered service must be credited with the hours of service that would have been performed but for the military absence, which are added to actual hours worked during the previous 12 months to satisfy the 1,250-hour requirement (subject to § 825.801(c) for airline flight crews).

To calculate the hours of service an employee would have worked during a USERRA-covered absence, the employer may generally use the employee's pre-service work schedule as the basis for the calculation, subject to special rules in § 825.801(c) for airline flight crews.

If an employer fails to maintain accurate records of an employee's hours worked (including for FLSA-exempt executive, administrative, and professional employees under 29 CFR part 541), the burden of proof is on the employer to show that the employee has not worked the required 1,250 hours.

Where accurate hours records are not maintained, the employer must be able to clearly demonstrate that full-time teachers at an educational establishment did not work 1,250 hours in the prior 12 months in order to deny FMLA eligibility on hours grounds (subject to § 825.801(d) for airline flight crews).

The determination of whether an employee satisfies both the 12-month length of service and the 1,250 hours of service requirements must be evaluated as of the date the requested FMLA leave is scheduled to begin.

If an employee is already on non-FMLA leave when reaching the 12-month employment threshold, any subsequent portion of the leave taken for an FMLA-qualifying reason after meeting that threshold becomes designated as FMLA leave.
The requirement that 50 employees work within 75 miles of the employee's worksite must be assessed at the specific time the employee gives notice of the need for leave.

Regardless of whether leave is taken all at once or on an intermittent or reduced leave schedule, once an employee is determined eligible based on notice, subsequent decreases or increases in employee count within 75 miles cannot alter the employee's eligibility for that specific notice of need for leave.
An employer is prohibited from terminating an employee's FMLA leave that has already commenced if the number of employees employed within 75 miles subsequently drops below 50.

Where an employer has 60 employees within 75 miles when notice is given in August, it must grant FMLA benefits to an otherwise eligible employee even if the employee count is expected to decrease to 40 when the leave begins in December.
